subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: If n is a positive integer, show that (1 + i)ⁿ + (1 − i)ⁿ = 2^((n+2)/2) cos(nπ/4).

mark_split.label: Raise to n by De Moivre's theorem
Add and combine the powers of 2

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — how you write 1 + i, what De Moivre's theorem does to it, and how the two powers of 2 combine at the end.
insider_note: The last line is where the mark goes: 2 times 2 to the n/2 is 2 to the (n + 2)/2, not 2 to the n. Write the exponent addition out.

steps.label: Mod-amp form of 1 + i
steps.margin_note: First and second marks. For 1 + i: r = √(1 + 1) = √2 and tan θ = 1, so θ = π/4, with x and y both positive. The √2 outside the bracket is what produces the power of 2 in the answer.
steps.memory_tip: r = √2 and θ = π/4. The √2 outside the bracket is what produces the power of 2.
lines: Let 1 + i = x + iy ⇒ x = 1, y = 1

recall.must_convey: That 1 + i is first written in modulus-amplitude form: r = √2 and θ = π/4, giving r(cos θ + i sin θ).
accept: first write 1 + i in mod amp form with r equal to √2 and theta equal to π/4
find the modulus and the amplitude of 1 + i and write it as r cos theta plus i sin theta
convert 1 + i to polar form r cis theta before raising the power
1 + i ni mod amp form lo rasi r √2 theta π/4 teeskovali
modulus amplitude form first, r is √2 and the angle is π/4

steps.why: De Moivre's theorem works only on a number written as cos θ + i sin θ. Pulling out r first is what makes the theorem usable, so this line is the method, not a preliminary.
common_mistakes: Writing r = 1 by habit; here r is not 1, and it is what produces the power of 2 in the answer.
Taking θ from tan θ without checking the quadrant: both x and y are positive, so θ is in the first quadrant.
Forgetting the r outside the bracket when the form is written.

steps.label: Raise to n by De Moivre
steps.margin_note: Third and fourth marks. The power n gives (√2)ⁿ and the angle nπ/4. Write (√2)ⁿ as 2 to the power n/2 on this line — the exponent in the final answer is built by adding to it.
steps.memory_tip: Write (√2)ⁿ as 2 to the power n/2 on this line — the final exponent is built by adding to it.

recall.must_convey: That De Moivre's theorem is applied: raising the mod-amp form to the power n multiplies the angle by n and gives 2 to the n by 2 times (cos(nπ/4) + i sin(nπ/4)), called equation (1).
accept: apply De Moivre's theorem so the angle is multiplied by n and we get 2 to the n by 2 times (cos(nπ/4) + i sin(nπ/4))
raise the mod amp form to the power and multiply the angle by n by De Moivre
by De Moivre cos theta plus i sin theta to the power gives cos n theta plus i sin n theta
De Moivre theorem apply chesi angle ni n tho multiply cheyyali
the power goes onto the angle by De Moivre's theorem, that is equation one

steps.why: De Moivre's theorem says (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ for every integer n: the power moves onto the angle. The real factor r is raised separately, as an ordinary real number.
common_mistakes: Raising √2 to n and leaving it as (√2)ⁿ instead of 2 to the power n/2, which is needed for the final power.
Multiplying the angle by 2n instead of n.
Writing (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cosⁿ θ + i sinⁿ θ, which is false.

steps.label: The conjugate power
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. 1 − i is the conjugate of 1 + i, so raising it to n gives the same 2 to the power n/2 with the sine sign reversed. Label it (2); nothing is recomputed.
steps.memory_tip: Same modulus factor, sine sign reversed. Nothing is recomputed.

recall.must_convey: That the conjugate number is treated in the same way and gives 2 to the n by 2 times (cos(nπ/4) − i sin(nπ/4)), called equation (2), with the sign of the sine term changed.
accept: similarly the conjugate gives the same thing with minus i sin, that is equation two
do the same for the conjugate and only the sign of the sine changes
the second bracket is the conjugate so its power is 2 to the n by 2 times (cos(nπ/4) − i sin(nπ/4))
conjugate ki same step, sin term sign matrame minus avuthundi
equation two is the conjugate with cos minus i sin

steps.why: The second number is the conjugate of the first, so it has the same r and the angle −θ. Nothing new has to be computed; only the sign of the sine changes.
common_mistakes: Changing the sign of the cosine as well as the sine.
Recomputing r and θ from scratch and losing time.
Writing equation (2) without the minus sign, so nothing cancels in the next step.

steps.label: Add (1) and (2)
steps.margin_note: Sixth and seventh marks. Adding (1) and (2) gives 2 to the power n/2 multiplied by 2 cos(nπ/4). Add the exponents: 1 + n/2 = (n + 2)/2, so the factor is 2 to the power (n + 2)/2, not 2ⁿ.
steps.memory_tip: Add the exponents, do not multiply: 1 + n/2 = (n + 2)/2, so the factor is 2^((n+2)/2), not 2ⁿ.

recall.must_convey: That equations (1) and (2) are added, the i sin terms cancel, and the result is 2 to the power (n + 2)/2 times cos(nπ/4).
accept: add one and two, the i sin terms cancel and we get 2 to the power (n + 2)/2 times cos(nπ/4)
adding the two equations the sine parts cancel leaving two times the cosine
one plus two gives two cos and the final answer is 2 to the power (n + 2)/2 times cos(nπ/4)
rendu equations add cheste sin terms cancel ayyi 2 to the power (n + 2)/2 times cos(nπ/4) vasthundi
the imaginary parts cancel on adding and the answer is two to the n plus one times cos

steps.why: The two numbers are conjugates, so their sum is twice the real part. Adding removes the i sin terms and leaves exactly the cosine the question asks for.
common_mistakes: Writing 2 · 2 to the n/2 as 2 to the n instead of adding the exponents: 1 + n/2 = (n + 2)/2.
Subtracting instead of adding, which leaves 2i sin instead of 2 cos.
Dropping the factor that comes from r = √2.
